rationale: All published cases of the mild/spastic paraplegia presentation of NFU1 deficiency (SPG93) tested for amino acids—including the index patient described by Tonduti et al. (2015) and the infant reported by Uzunhan et al. (2020)—demonstrated elevated glycine in plasma/serum, driven mechanistically by impaired lipoylation of the glycine cleavage system H-protein. This biochemical signature sharply distinguishes it from classical uncomplicated and complicated HSPs (such as SPG4, SPG7, and SPG11), in which glycine metabolism is unaffected. However, broader reviews of iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis and lipoic acid synthesis defects (Selvanathan & Sankaran 2022) note that patients 'can have' raised glycine and lactate rather than exhibiting invariable, constant 100% penetrance across all clinical stages. Furthermore, because fewer than a dozen SPG93 individuals have been comprehensively phenotyped biochemically, asserting absolute (100%) sensitivity is statistically underpowered and challenged by reports showing intermittent or variable metabolic perturbations in milder mitochondrial hypomorphs.

evidence.text: A patient with adult-onset slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, cognitive impairment, and leukoencephalopathy harboring NFU1 mutations exhibited persistent high glycine concentration in body fluids.

conflicts: General reviews of ISC biogenesis disorders indicate that elevated body-fluid glycine and lactate are variable ('can have raised plasma and CSF glycine') rather than documented as 100% obligate across every single clinical draw and phenotype.

The total number of published SPG93 (milder/spastic paraplegia NFU1) patients tested biochemically remains extremely small (n < 15), meaning statistical confidence for absolute 100% sensitivity cannot be validated against prospective cohorts.

new_directions.question_text: What is the systematic sensitivity of fasting plasma glycine versus urinary organic acids and CSF amino acid panels in adult and late-onset hypomorphic NFU1 alleles?
new_directions.rationale: Because hypomorphic NFU1 alleles retain partial Fe-S transfer activity, plasma glycine levels may fluctuate with dietary protein intake or intercurrent catabolic stress, which could lead to false-negative single-timepoint screens.

new_directions.question_text: Does neuroimaging (cavitating frontal leukoencephalopathy and spinal cord atrophy) combined with serum glycine achieve 100% specificity when discriminating SPG93 from SPG11, SPG7, and secondary MS mimics?
new_directions.rationale: SPG11 can show thin corpus callosum with periventricular white matter changes, but lacking cavitating leukoencephalopathy and hyperglycinemia, determining the exact multiparametric diagnostic rule would prevent misdiagnoses.
